messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 35
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Divorced
- Occupation: Accountant
- Trauma Type: Torture
- Pcl5: 57

**Patient Vignette: Mr. L.**

Mr. L. is a 35-year-old, divorced South Eastern Asian man who works as an accountant for a mid-sized firm. He presents as meticulously dressed, his posture rigid, his hands clasped tightly in his lap. He speaks in a low, measured tone, often pausing to scan the room before answering a question.

The events that reshaped his life began five years ago, during a business trip to his home country. He was there to audit a joint venture. One evening, after leaving his office, he was bundled into a van by men in plain clothes. He was taken to a nondescript building and held for three days. The men accused him of embezzling from the company, a charge he insists was fabricated to pressure his employer. They did not demand money. They demanded information. They wanted him to sign a false statement implicating his boss in a political scandal.

He describes the torture as methodical. He was beaten with a rubber hose, his head forced underwater until he choked, and he was subjected to electrical shocks to his hands and feet. The worst part, he says, was the isolation and the uncertainty. "I didn't know if I would be killed or released," he tells me, his eyes fixed on a spot on the floor. "I just wanted it to stop. I would have said anything." He signed the document on the third day. They released him at dawn, dumped on a roadside outside the city, his wallet and passport returned. He flew home the next day.

In the months that followed, Mr. L. tried to bury the experience. He told no one, not even his then-wife. He threw himself into his work, the columns of numbers a refuge from the chaos in his mind. But the refuge soon collapsed. He became hypervigilant. In the office, the sudden sound of a co-worker clearing his throat would make him flinch. A door slamming in the hallway would send a jolt of adrenaline through him, his heart hammering against his ribs. He began to avoid the open-plan area, preferring the isolated quiet of a back storage room to eat his lunch.

The nightmares started six months after the event. He would wake in a cold sweat, gasping for air, the sensation of the wet cloth over his face still vivid. He began to drink heavily to fall asleep. His wife, confused by his irritability and emotional distance, accused him of having an affair. He could not explain. The shame was a physical weight. He could not tell her that he had been broken, that he had signed a lie to save his own skin. The marriage dissolved within two years.

Now, Mr. L. lives alone in a sterile, one-bedroom apartment. His life is a series of rituals. He checks the locks on his door three times before going to bed. He always sits with his back to the wall in restaurants. He cannot tolerate being touched unexpectedly. At work, his performance has declined. He struggles to concentrate, his mind drifting back to the windowless room. He has been written up twice for missing deadlines. His boss, a kind man, has expressed concern, but Mr. L. dismisses it as "just stress."

He tells me he feels hollow. "I am a calculator," he says. "I process numbers. But I don't feel anything anymore." He has stopped going out with friends. He has no hobbies. The only emotion that surfaces with regularity is a pervasive, low-grade dread. He is afraid of the dark. He is afraid of closed doors. Most of all, he is afraid of the memory, which feels not like a memory of a past event, but like a present, ongoing violation. He carries the weight of that room with him, every minute of every day, a silent, invisible torture that never ended. He came to therapy not because he wants to feel better, but because he is exhausted.
